lesson.title: Dissenters at Home: The Fight Against American Empire
lesson.summary: Founded in 1898, the Anti-Imperialist League brought together an unusual coalition of prominent Americans who argued that colonizing the Philippines betrayed the nation's founding principles of self-government.
lesson.body:
Even as the United States moved to annex the Philippines, a significant number of Americans objected loudly to the whole idea of overseas empire, and in 1898 opponents in Boston organized the American Anti-Imperialist League to give that opposition a coordinated voice. The League drew members from across the political spectrum who otherwise agreed on very little, including the writer Mark Twain, the industrialist Andrew Carnegie, the labor leader Samuel Gompers, former president Grover Cleveland, and the philosopher William James, united mainly by a shared discomfort with what the acquisition of the Philippines said about the country's direction.

Their arguments were varied but overlapped in important ways. Many argued from principle, insisting that a nation founded on the consent of the governed had no business ruling millions of Filipinos who had never consented to American rule, a direct contradiction, they said, of the ideals in the Declaration of Independence. Others worried about the practical costs of empire, fearing that governing a distant colonial population would require a large standing military and entangle the United States in expensive, open-ended conflicts, fears that seemed to be confirmed almost immediately by the outbreak of the Philippine-American War following the Philippines acquisition. Still others voiced racial anxieties, arguing that incorporating a large non-white population would create problems at home rather than out of any deep commitment to Filipino self-rule, a reminder that opposition to empire did not always come from purely egalitarian motives.

Despite its prominent membership, the League ultimately lost the political fight. The Senate ratified the Treaty of Paris in early 1899, and the United States went on to fight and win the Philippine-American War, retaining control of the islands until granting independence decades later, in 1946. The League's efforts did not reverse American policy, but they left a lasting record of principled dissent, showing that the turn toward overseas empire was contested from the very beginning rather than accepted as an obvious or unanimous national choice.
